newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic to win elections but lose credibility.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic to win elections but lose credibility.

text.p: Opposition leaders urged voters to boycott the third round of disputed municipal elections on Wednesday, clearing the way for Yugoslavia's ruling Socialists to retain power tainted by allegations of electoral fraud.

The authorities used the courts to annul clear opposition victories, which the socialists at first admitted, in Belgrade and industrial towns across Serbia that President Slobodan Milosevic could not afford to lose.
Reversing the outcome denied the opposition its first grasp of power in modern Yugoslavia but left Milosevic's democratic credentials in ruins.
Western ambassadors met Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic at the weekend to stress their governments' dismay over the way the Socialists bulldozed embarrassing election results aside.

"The astonishing thing is that this was ever allowed to happen," one envoy said on condition of anonymity. "After all, it is the authorities who control the electoral process and who count the votes."
Milosevic's socialists had already won a convincing victory in federal elections this month which coincided with the first round of the municipal poll.
Political commentators in Belgrade said it would have been relatively convincing to claim that the municipal vote followed the same trend as the federal ballot.

There was puzzlement that Socialist leaders freely acknowledged after the second round 10 days ago that they had lost Belgrade while the opposition claimed to have won in other industrial strongholds that are supposed to be the bedrock of working class support for Milosevic.
It was only after the scale of his first serious electoral defeat became evident that the Socialists began to rewrite the result. Milosevic sacked the head of state television as a first scapegoat.
The fiasco destroyed an elaborate facade Milosevic had constructed since turning the old Yugoslav communist machine into a Socialist Party apparently competing in a multi-party democracy.

Although Milosevic held the reins, the socialists often secured their electoral victories in coalition with leftist allies to avoid looking as if they monopolised the system in the communist tradition.
Suspicions have been aroused in the past by the speed with which the parliamentary representation of parties allied to the socialists has waxed and waned according to Milosevic's needs.
The opposition seized on the legal manipulations to deprive them of their victory as proof that the multi-party system is window-dressing for total political control by the Socialists.
Although the opposition has mounted noisy, if ineffectual, demonstrations, no one doubts that Milosevic will get his way, however tarnished his party's legitimacy.
The opposition go into every election claiming to to be buoyed by their chances of victory, but the reality is that the socialists cannot afford to lose.

Milosevic and other senior socialists would risk being called to account for their role in the disintegration of old Yugoslavia and the corruption and economic impovrishment which have been rife since.
One of the first acts of an opposition government would be to dismantle the Socialists' control of the Yugoslav media, which has been crucial to maintaining their power.
Political sources said the municipal debacle could force Milosevic to delay plans to call Serbian republican elections in March.

These are not due until December 1997 but are important to consolidating his political future for the next decade, and political sources said the socialists' success in the federal poll had tempted him to settle the republican elections.

The sources expected Milosevic to arrange the outcome so that two allied parties, the Marxist United Left of Yugoslavia (YUL) and New Democracy (ND) would between them solve the potentially explosive issues of privatisation and Kosovo.

This scenario would shelter the socialists from any resulting unpopularity while leaving Milosevic in full control and the option of moving towards a future powerbase that included the moderate opposition.

The sources said the handling of the municipal vote made it less likely Yugoslavs would be convinced by the results of republican elections or that any opposition party could risk cooperation with Milosevic.
